items.stem: A generated C# method triggers a nullable reference warning. The correct response is to:

options.text: Address the null-safety issue the warning identifies, not suppress it blindly
options.rationale: Correct: nullable warnings flag real null-handling gaps that should be resolved.

options.text: Disable nullable reference types for the whole project
options.rationale: Disabling the feature hides genuine null-safety issues.

options.text: Add a pragma to suppress it without understanding it
options.rationale: Blind suppression leaves the underlying risk in place.

options.text: Ignore it because the code compiles
options.rationale: A warning can precede a real NullReferenceException at runtime.

items.explanation: Correct: nullable warnings flag real null-handling gaps that should be resolved.

items.stem: Which TWO are appropriate ways to verify a .NET change before shipping it? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run dotnet build and confirm no new analyzer warnings
options.rationale: Correct: a clean analyzed build is a baseline quality gate.

options.text: Run the affected project's tests with dotnet test
options.rationale: Correct: targeted tests confirm the change behaves as intended.

options.text: Confirm the file count in the project increased
options.rationale: File count is not a correctness signal.

options.text: Ask Claude Code to assert that it is confident
options.rationale: A model's confidence is not verification.

items.explanation: Correct: a clean analyzed build is a baseline quality gate.

items.stem: An xUnit test fails after a change. Claude Code suggests editing the test's expected value to match the new output. This is wrong because:

options.text: It may hide the defect the test correctly detected rather than fixing the cause
options.rationale: Correct: changing the assertion to pass can mask a real regression.

options.text: xUnit tests can never be edited
options.rationale: Tests can be edited when the requirement legitimately changed.

options.text: Tests always take priority over code
options.rationale: Neither blindly wins; the point is to fix the true cause.
Writability is not the issue; correctness of the fix is.

items.explanation: Correct: changing the assertion to pass can mask a real regression.
